affiliate links unless marked. minimize view to: item links show all: setup breakdown - gaming monitor: rog swift oled pg27aqdp | $999.00 resolution: 2560x1440p refresh rate: 480hz picked up an asus rog swift oled pg27aqdp 480hz 1440p oled in december 2024. it's primarily used for counter-strike 2, but i'll definitely be playing most of my games on it. so far, i've really enjoyed it. there's a huge difference between this monitor and my previous 280hz 1080p display. the motion clarity and response times are insane. the higher pixel density is also incredibly useful in cs2 for long-range duels. on most maps in cs2, with a 4090 + 7800x3d at native resolution, fps averages between 500-700 fps (depending on the map and settings). when the monitor dips below 480hz, it's not very noticeable. occasionally, there are some minor motion artifacts due to frame rate fluctuations, but the response time is fast enough to not affect gameplay. if your pc or wallet isn't ready for this monitor, a 360hz 1440p oled could get you close to this level of performance for a fraction of the price, though 480hz still provides a small edge in competitive play. i have tried out g-sync and elmb but prefer both of them off as it just feels better without them. if anyone plays on stretched resolution with full-screen windowed mode, it can be difficult to get the monitor to consistently stay at a custom resolution due to issues with dsc. it is possible by disabling dsc, creating a custom resolution in the nvidia 3d settings, then re-enabling dsc. however, any time you turn off the monitor, you will have to set the resolution again. to avoid dsc altogether, you will need a gpu with displayport 2.1, which is included on most 50-series nvidia cards but is harder to find on other gpu models. i tend to change my in-game resolution quite frequently because i'm a placebo settings changer. as of march 2025, i'm playing in 16:10 fullscreen, which is running very smoothly. when i first bought the monitor, i was using the native resolution (2560x1440p), but i felt like switching it up and trying stretched for a while. personally, i have no real resolution preference-it just depends on what i'm feeling that day, and i can usually adjust to a new resolution on the same day i change it. i would say half of my hours are on 16:10 and the other half on other resolutions like 16:9, 4:3, and 16:9 stretched on my ultrawide monitor. this monitor also takes up two internal gpu ports, leaving you with three external gpu ports (displayport, hdmi, etc.). if you use four or more monitors, you will need to use your integrated graphics for one monitor or install another gpu. i was able to get this monitor on sale for $995.72, including taxes and shipping. i waited for over a year and saved accordingly, using my end-of-year bonus to afford this monitor. normally, with tax, it would have cost $1,068.93, so i saved $73.21 in total from the sale. now, the most important question: is this monitor worth the price? this monitor is on the bleeding edge of technology and will give you a competitive advantage over opponents through the ability to react a few milliseconds quicker. better motion clarity, response time, and pixel density all contribute to improved reaction speed with this monitor. i spend a good chunk of my day in front of this monitor and enjoy trying out the newest tech. if you have a pc capable of powering this monitor, use that pc for highly competitive games for hours a day, and have some extra money to spare, this monitor is definitely worth experiencing. alternatively, if your pc or budget isn't ready for this monitor, a 360hz 1440p oled could get you close to this level of performance at a fraction of the cost. overall, if you're impatient and want peak performance asap, buy this monitor. otherwise, in 1-2 years, this monitor should go on sale, and more competition should emerge at lower prices. insane motion clarity and response times. higher pixel density improves visibility in long-range fights. fps averages 500-700 on high-end hardware. some ghosting may occur when fps dips below 480hz. dsc can cause resolution issues in fullscreen windowed mode. requires two internal gpu ports, limiting connectivity. expensive, but may go on sale in the future. - ultrawide monitor: lg 34wl850 | $699.00 resolution: 3440x1440p refresh rate: 60hz having an ultrawide monitor is amazing for productivity. coding, editing videos, and using photoshop are all much better with the extra screen real estate. watching movies is also really enjoyable, as many movies with black bars can be stretched to take up the entire monitor. at the time when i purchased it, it was quite expensive, but it was the only ultrawide i could find that could receive a display signal via usb-c and had two usb-3 connectors to work as a usb hub for my laptop. although i no longer use a laptop as my main computer, this monitor still comes in handy anytime i am not playing video games. - other displays: asus 24" monitor | $119.00 resolution: 1920x1080p refresh rate: 60hz response time: 2ms i have had two of these 24-inch asus monitors for over 10 years now. they have been more than been worth it to me. they were my original gaming monitors, and although they were 60hz, their 2ms response time was quite fast for the time. i have used these monitors as secondary displays for quite a few years now. the brightness and contrast are not as good as they used to be, but they still turn on after many, many hours of use, so i cannot complain! - mouse: custom logitech g pro x superlight wireless | $159.99 modified g pro superlight mouse i've customized my g pro superlight with a hotswap pcb board, ttc 60 million gold switches, a bandaid mod for the side buttons, a weight reduction mod, and wallhack obsidian dot skates. the hotswap pcb works great and is compatible with the stock superlight scroll wheel. the scroll wheel steps feel much more distinct and less mushy compared to stock. i really enjoy the ttc gold 60m switches-they feel significantly faster than the stock ones. having a hotswap pcb is a huge plus since it lets me try different switches anytime without needing to solder. the bandaid mod involves cutting small pieces of a bandaid and placing them under the side button switches. this improves the feel, making the clicks more responsive and reducing the actuation distance. for weight reduction, i removed excess plastic using a wire cutter and a handheld rotary tool. i also took out the powerplay module and trimmed unnecessary plastic around the frame. i've used stock skates for a few years and tried tiger ice skates for a while. both performed well, but after upgrading to a glass mouse pad, i needed something more durable. the wallhack obsidian dot skates feel similar to tiger ice in terms of friction, but since they have a much smaller surface area, they glide more smoothly. the obsidian skates package includes plenty of extra skates, so i'm not too worried about wear and tear. also added a magnetic micro usb charger. this plugs into the existing port and allows the mouse to easily connect to a magnetic charger without having to manually align the original charger. this makes it extremely easy to plug in and encourages me to plug in my mouse when not using it. it does add around a gram of weight to the front of the mouse but the convenience of easily plugging in the mouse is more than worth the added weight. i'm using the stock battery. i really considered swapping out the battery for a smaller and lighter alternative but i really enjoyed only having to charge the mouse like once a week, so decided to stick with the stock battery. - mouse pad: wallhack sp-004 | official store so far, this glass mousepad has done everything i need it to do. it might sound a little crazy, but the main reason i got this mousepad is because of how easy it is to clean. a traditional mousepad is a magnet for dust and grime, which i have found to seriously affect the consistency of my aim. a glass mousepad is extremely easy to wipe off with a microfiber cloth, and i always keep a few handy next to my desk. the base of this mousepad is great-it does not move around at all and will not damage the desk. i do think that the "performance" of a glass mousepad is overrated and that the skates on your mouse itself have a larger effect on the speed and friction while moving your mouse. one annoyance that i have heard other people talk about, and that i agree with, is how loud it is when swiping with your mouse. it may seem ridiculous to complain about the sound of a $120 mousepad, but with open-back headphones, it is loud enough to cover up some important but quiet footsteps in counter-strike. overall, i think that this mousepad was worth the high price because of its easy-to-clean surface, and it shouldn't need to be replaced as often as a traditional mousepad. - keyboard: wooting 60he | prices on build list i have had this wooting 60he since late spring 2023 and absolutely love it. i have spent way too much time and money trying out different mods. full parts list and breakdown on the keyboard tab! - monitor arms: wallhack sp-004 | official store i have used three different monitor arms, all of which are desk clamp-mounted. my favorite monitor arm is a gas spring arm. i own the discontinued amazon basics model, which, at the time of purchase, was the cheapest available pneumatic arm. nowadays, these types of arms are much more affordable. it allows you to position your monitor however you want, with no major constraints on height, depth, or rotation. i also have an extra-tall monitor arm that allows for 36 inches of height. it comes with three detachable sections and is relatively sturdy for its height. there is some wobble, but that is to be expected when mounting a monitor so high. the remaining two monitor arms are affordable arms that allow swivel, tilt and rotation but not height adjustment. these arms have held up great for the price, with only a little sag over a few years but otherwise have outperformed my expectations - headphones: beyerdynamic dt 990 pro 250 ohm (limited edition black) | $179.99 i have had these headphones since 2023 and really enjoy them. they perform really well with music and gaming. i would suggest having something other than your pc to power them. for years i used a sound blaster z internal amp/dac, but since purchasing the streamer x use it to power these headphones. these headphones are open back which are great for sound quality but you can hear everything in the outside world through them, which is a bit annoying if you have noisy neighbors. also if your volume is too high and your microphone is too close, your headphones audio will be picked up by your microphone. - microphone: shure sm7b | $399.00 - audio interface: rode streamer x | $249.99 so far, the rode streamer x accomplishes what it needs to do. it functions as an amp for the shure sm7b microphone, providing power and a gain knob. it also features a headphone volume knob, which is really helpful for adjusting the volume. one of the main deciding factors in purchasing this device was the hdmi capture card, which allows me to connect my sony zv-e10 mirrorless camera. a lot of my teammates get a kick out of the voice effects, such as the chipmunk and robot voices. although it does what i need it to do, the software is definitely a struggle to work with. rode central does not save your settings after restarting your pc unless you replace the file generated by the program, and sometimes the hdmi capture card struggles to pick up the signal from my mirrorless camera. - microphone arm: elgato wave mic arm | $99.00 the elgato wave mic arm is very high quality. it has more than enough lift to handle the shure sm7b and actually needs the included counter weight to keep the arm from raising on it's own. i prefer to have my mic mounted high up and out of the way of the desk's surface. many people prefer low profile mic arm's but having a 7 foot wingspan, i could see myself bumping into the low profile arm, as well as knocking over beverages since it is mounted so low. the cable management channels included on the top and back of the arm are really clean and super easy to open in case you need to adjust or swap out your microphone cable. i'm using the included height spacer as well, so my arm is mounted at its max height and i have never run into any issues with it being in the way. as of right now i have zero complaints about this mic stand and have found it well worth the money - camera: sony zv-e10 | $798.00 i have been using this camera for a few years now and it does it's job well. it is the main camera in all of my youtube content and i plan to use it for the foreseeable future. i was originally using the included kit lens but it did not perform very well indoors, which is where i primarily use this camera. with the kit lens you had to increase the iso to a very high setting to see anything, but this would result in very grainy videos/photos. i eventually picked up a sigma 16mm f/1.4 lens, and it performed really well in low light conditions for quite a while i used the included "webcam" feature on the zve10. this allowed you to plug the camera into your computer with a usb-c cable and use it as a webcam. this feature worked pretty well but could only output at 1080p i upgraded to an elgato cam link 4k that allows the zve10 to output signal through its min hdmi cable for a while. when i purchased the rode streamer x, i no longer needed the elgato cam link, since the streamer x had a capture card i could use - web cam: logitech logitech c920 | $99.00 - web cam arm: suspension boom scissor mic arm | $18.99 gator frameworks camera mount mic stand adapter with ball-and-socket head | $10.99 - key light: godox es45 | $99.00 this key light serves a couple of really important purposes for me. the main purpose of this key light is to provide artificial day light for purposes of energy and focus. i'm a big fan of the huberman lab podcast and one major point he hammers home is getting adequate light in your eyes to stimulate your bodies natural response to be awake. of course the second purpose of this key light is to provide lighting for photos/videos and it does a really good job the godox es45 comes with a portable remote with knobs to control the brightness and color temperature that sits on my desk and is powered by micro usb. i also have this light setup with a wifi enabled outlet that automatically turns on at the same time of my alarm to wake up. having a bright light is very helpful for waking up in the morning. - desk: flexispot e6 desk sit stand up desk (black frame + bamboo desktop) | $449.39 (on sale) so far, i have really enjoyed this desk. at its max height, it works well with a walking pad, and i'm very tall at 6'7". before purchasing this desk, i heard some reviews say that there was some wobble at its max height, but so far, i have not found it to be an issue, and it does not wobble much at all. it is really nice to be able to adjust the height when i'm eating food, as i like to have it a bit higher in case anything falls off the fork. the desk lets you set four different height buttons. my settings are as follows: standing button: max height 49.2" sitting button: 31.1" button 3: eating height 35" button 4: minimum height 23.6" my black desk is an old ikea desk that is over a decade old. it is quite sturdy but they no longer sell this model. i have also used the "thicker" ikea desk models, but they are hollow on the inside and are about as sturdy as cardboard. - walking pad: deerrun walking pad | $129.99 this treadmill has been extremely useful during the winter. it gets way too cold where i live, so having the option to hop on this walkpad for a few miles a day helps keep me active. i tend to walk on it when doing light productivity tasks, watching youtube, or a movie. i like to set it on its lowest setting if i'm doing some productive work, but if i am just watching a movie, i will put it somewhere between 1.5 and 2.2 mph, which, at the higher end, can work up a sweat after a mile or two. during the winter, i would try to get five miles a day throughout the day, usually in increments of 1-2 miles. overall, i think this is one of my best purchases, as it significantly increases activity levels and has more than paid for itself! gaming setup with ultra wide monitor, 3 16:9 monitors, and a 50 inch tv. five screens total. 2023 gaming setup with 2 monitors tv wooting keyboard pc in background gaming setup with 2 monitors tv wooting keyboard pc in background bottom side of superlight mouse with skates and cut out bottom for weight wallhack glass mouse pad with g pro superlight sitting on top keyboard case that looks like cs2 kilowatt case dt990 pro headphones rode streamer x audio interface godox es45 key light controller gear: desk with productivity and gaming, lights on

entries.text: programs | owen miner programs owen uses: coding stack (cursor, codex, claude, antigravity, ollama), adobe creative cloud, gimp, obs, and open-source multi-streaming. programs software i actually open: coding, creative work, and streaming. disclosure: this page includes a cursor referral link (50% off the first month for new users) that may also grant credits to both of us. eligibility and amounts are set by cursor on their site. thanks for supporting the channel. nothing here is paid sponsorship; it is the honest split of what sits on disk when work needs to get done (one cursor refer-a-friend link is in the cursor card below). coding & development this site is html, css, and a little browser javascript. on cursor pro+ ($60/mo as of may 2026) to finish it; chatgpt for planning; gemini for everyday q&a. i tried openclaw on ubuntu in a vm. interesting, but api spend added up fast; local-only was not enough for the heavy lifting i need right now. editor cursor primary ide + agent workspace 50% off first month: cursor referral new users · code axmcfhz8a2dg cursor is my main editor: multi-file edits, refactors, this repo, and the integrated agent on real paths. i upgraded to pro+ so hosted models and agents have enough headroom to finish the site without constantly bouncing to other tools. fallback codex (openai) backup when cursor limits bite when i hit cursor usage limits, codex-style workflows are the first fallback. i use visual studio code for that lane. for codex together with cloud-oriented integrations, i reach for full visual studio instead (same family of tools, different shell depending on whether i am in a light editor session or a heavier vs + cloud setup). assistant claude paused, may come back i gave the claude app and the visual studio integrations a real try. the experience was solid, but the lower paid tier ran out of usage too quickly for what i was doing, so i canceled for now. i might resubscribe later, especially after seeing premiere pro integrations show up (the adobe video tool is covered below), which looked genuinely useful. for claude-shaped help today i lean on antigravity via the gemini stack instead of a standalone claude subscription. third lane antigravity + gemini third option & everyday answers antigravity is my third lane after cursor and codex when i want another angle or a more exploratory pass, including mockups and “what if” ui that might not ship. the gemini subscription also opens claude there, which covers some of what i used to route to a standalone claude plan. separately, i use gemini all the time for quick general q&a outside project files, not a replacement for cursor, but a natural first stop for questions. local ollama offline drafts on the rtx box ollama on the rtx box handles the local grunt work: first drafts, repetitive transforms, and summaries, so hosted quotas last longer. cloud models still win when the task needs stronger reasoning; local is deliberately “good enough to verify,” not a substitute for everything. adobe creative cloud & design most serious photo and video work lives in creative cloud. video-wise, my first editor was the one bundled with windows (the simple built-in timeline app, where i cut my teeth first). in my early teens i bought sony vegas movie studio on amazon and moved my edits there; i was deep into youtube and making videos at the time. today premiere pro carries that thread (exact purchase dates from back then tbd when i dig them up). on stills i leaned on gimp early when photoshop was not in the budget. video premiere pro editing & finishing premiere pro is where most of my video editing happens now (timelines, color passes, exports for social and long-form) after years that started with windows’ bundled editor and vegas movie studio. it pairs with the rest of the stack when a project needs to leave the nle and land on the site or a stream. raster photoshop still imaging & composites i use photoshop constantly: assets for the site, thumbnails, cleanup, and layers-on-layers work i have been doing since i was young. it is the default when pixels need to be precise. motion after effects learning: projection & motion i want to go deeper on after effects, especially for motion pieces that feed projection mapping and immersive visuals. that future setup is sketched on my upgrades page (full-apartment ideas). ae is the logical tool for map-aligned content and animated plates before they hit the projectors. foss gimp where i started before i could justify creative cloud, gimp carried most of my raster work. i still respect it. it taught me a lot of the same habits i use in photoshop today. if budget is tight, gimp remains a capable option. streaming live video goes through obs studio, with an open-source multi-destination helper from github so i am not locked to a single rtmp endpoint. live obs studio capture & broadcast obs studio is my hub for streaming and recording: scenes, audio routing, cameras, and whatever needs to hit viewers in real time. everything else in this section plugs into or sits beside obs. oss multi rtmp open-source multi-stream (github) for streaming to more than one platform without relying only on paid relay services, i use the open-source obs multi rtmp plugin (sorayuki / obs-multi-rtmp on github). it adds multiple rtmp outputs from one obs session, handy when you want redundancy or simultaneous destinations. no api keys or account identifiers belong on a public page. store those in your own password manager and environment, not in git. the cursor referral link offers new users 50% off the first month and may earn credits for you and me; rewards and eligibility are controlled by cursor.

entries.text: counter strike background | gaming | owen miner counter-strike background: from community servers in 2015 to faceit level 10, premier leaderboard appearances, and cs content creation. ← gaming counter strike background i have been playing counter-strike since 2015. most of my time early on was in community servers, 1v1s, b-hop, and surf. i have always enjoyed the skin scene and had a lot of fun testing combos on community servers. toward the end of cs:go my peak competitive rank was supreme. i reached faceit level 10 in about 300 matches, in january 2024, a few months after cs2's release. since then i have mostly played premier and competitive; i love the goofy, chill environment and the people you run into. i have been on the premier leaderboard a few times but have found it hard to stay there with the cheater problem. in 2023 i started making cs:go shorts and tiktoks for fun and have since made some long-form youtube content. i still experiment with different formats when i have free time. i also make photoshop work you can find on my twitter / x page. feel free to ask me any questions you have in chat! peak premier rank 29,771 peak faceit elo 2312 view my leetify profile → last updated 7/10; check leetify for updated rank. first time hitting supreme (cs:go alt) don't tell valve, but i booted an old alt that had been master guardian, got placed at legendary eagle after not playing for a few years, then ranked to supreme within a day on short matches when i was locked in and winning. i moved back to my main to grind global; cs:go shut down before i got there. gaming setup with multiple displays cs:go rank screen, alt account placed at legendary eagle after inactivity cs:go rank-up to supreme on alt account using short matches cs:go supreme rank close-up on alt account cs:go supreme rank on alt, then switched to main to grind global before cs:go shutdown

entries.snippet: CS2 bug found and fixed: Dust II pixel gap. June 2024 video, Reddit, NartOutHere credit, Valve patch.
entries.text: cs2 bug found & fixed: dust ii pixel gap | gaming | owen miner cs2 bug found and fixed: dust ii pixel gap. june 2024 video, reddit, nartouthere credit, valve patch. ← gaming cs2 bug found & fixed: dust ii pixel gap documented june 28, 2024 · counter-strike 2 youtube (short, 9:16), 7,802 views · 176 likes reddit (r/globaloffensive), 172 upvotes · 14 comments heads up: this wall crack reveals your position on dust ii! in globaloffensive i recorded this tiny geometry gap on dust ii, the kind of spot you only notice when you’re lining up angles, and posted it on youtube and reddit (embedded above), and a few other places. at the time i meant to forward it through the same channel valve uses for counter-strike bug reports; i’m not 100% certain that email ever went out, but the intent was there. a day later (june 29, 2024), cs creator nartouthere featured the clip in 70 tips to become a better cs2 player at 6:32 (with on-screen credit) in a tips compilation. open the video on youtube or use the screenshot below, the still shows the “credit owenmcs” callout on the gap. ← watch nartouthere video here nartouthere (youtube), 21,789 views · 578 likes · uploaded jun 29, 2024 watch at 6:32 views last updated 5/2/2026 a few days after that, valve shipped the july 2, 2024 update , whose map notes included “fixed hole in brick stack on bombsite b” on dust ii, that closed this gap. i’ve sent valve quite a few reports over the years without seeing a clear match in patch notes. this was the first time i could point at an update and feel pretty confident that this little map fix was connected to the work i put out publicly, including that first video, so it’s a personal milestone even if the change was small on paper. my youtube · reddit · nartouthere (6:32) youtube screenshot: nartouthere’s 70 tips cs2 video on dust ii with credit owenmcs in the corner; 21,789 views and 578 likes.

before. vertical mount attempt (abandoned) tried mounting the 4090 vertically in the o11 dynamic evo, gave up after the riser cable was a dud (rma’d) and routing display cables plus the strimer was entries.text: audio interface, rode streamer x | gear | owen miner ← gear - audio interface: disclosure some links on this page are affiliate links. if you buy through them, owen miner may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. that support helps fund content on this website and social media. as an amazon associate i earn from qualifying purchases. rode streamer x | $249.99 so far, the rode streamer x accomplishes what it needs to do. it functions as an amp for the shure sm7b microphone, providing power and a gain knob. it also features a headphone volume knob, which is really helpful for adjusting the volume. one of the main deciding factors in purchasing this device was the hdmi capture card, which allows me to connect my sony zv-e10 mirrorless camera. a lot of my teammates get a kick out of the voice effects, such as the chipmunk and robot voices. although it does what i need it to do, i am not a huge fan of the companion software, it has been pretty glitchy, though updates have helped a little. for the price i wish it felt more polished: you are paying a lot for the hardware, but the software still matters day to day. rode central still does not save your settings after restarting your pc unless you replace the file generated by the program, and sometimes the hdmi capture card struggles to pick up the signal from my mirrorless camera. rode streamer x audio interface

product page (specs, not a shop): rog swift oled pg27aqdp. another retailer: newegg, asus pg27aqdp (not an affiliate link). resolution: 2560x1440p refresh rate: 480hz picked up an asus rog swift oled pg27aqdp 480hz 1440p oled in december 2024. it’s primarily used for counter-strike 2, but i’ll definitely be playing most of my games on it. so far, i’ve really enjoyed it. there’s a huge difference between this monitor and my previous 280hz 1080p display. the motion clarity and response times are insane. the higher pixel density is also incredibly useful in cs2 for long-range duels. on most maps in cs2, with a 4090 + 7800x3d at native resolution, fps averages between 500-700 fps (depending on the map and settings). when the monitor dips below 480hz, it’s not very noticeable. occasionally, there are some minor motion artifacts due to frame rate fluctuations, but the response time is fast enough to not affect gameplay. if your pc or wallet isn’t ready for this monitor, a 360hz 1440p oled could get you close to this level of performance for a fraction of the price, though 480hz still provides a small edge in competitive play. i have tried out g-sync and elmb but prefer both of them off as it just feels better without them. if anyone plays on stretched resolution with full-screen windowed mode, it can be difficult to get the monitor to consistently stay at a custom resolution due to issues with dsc. it is possible by disabling dsc, creating a custom resolution in the nvidia 3d settings, then re-enabling dsc. however, any time you turn off the monitor, you will have to set the resolution again. to avoid dsc altogether, you will need a gpu with displayport 2.1, which is included on most 50-series nvidia cards but is harder to find on other gpu models. i tend to change my in-game resolution quite frequently because i’m a placebo settings changer. as of march 2025, i’m playing in 16:10 fullscreen, which is running very smoothly. when i first bought the monitor, i was using the native resolution (2560x1440p), but i felt like switching it up and trying stretched for a while. personally, i have no real resolution preference, it just depends on what i’m feeling that day, and i can usually adjust to a new resolution on the same day i change it. i would say half of my hours are on 16:10 and the other half on other resolutions like 16:9, 4:3, and 16:9 stretched on my ultrawide monitor. this monitor also takes up two internal gpu ports, leaving you with three external gpu ports (displayport, hdmi, etc.). if you use four or more monitors, you will need to use your integrated graphics for one monitor or install another gpu. i was able to get this monitor on sale for $995.72, including taxes and shipping. i waited for over a year and saved accordingly, using my end-of-year bonus to afford this monitor. normally, with tax, it would have cost $1,068.93, so i saved $73.21 in total from the sale. now, the most important question: is this monitor worth the price? this monitor is on the bleeding edge of technology and will give you a competitive advantage over opponents through the ability to react a few milliseconds quicker. better motion clarity, response time, and pixel density all contribute to improved reaction speed with this monitor. i spend a good chunk of my day in front of this monitor and enjoy trying out the newest tech. if you have a pc capable of powering this monitor, use that pc for highly competitive games for hours a day, and have some extra money to spare, this monitor is definitely worth experiencing. alternatively, if your pc or budget isn’t ready for this monitor, a 360hz 1440p oled could get you close to this level of performance at a fraction of the cost. overall, if you're impatient and want peak performance asap, buy this monitor. otherwise, in 1-2 years, this monitor should go on sale, and more competition should emerge at lower prices. insane motion clarity and response times. higher pixel density improves visibility in long-range fights. fps averages 500-700 on high-end hardware. some ghosting may occur when fps dips below 480hz. dsc can cause resolution issues in fullscreen windowed mode. requires two internal gpu ports, limiting connectivity. expensive, but may go on sale in the future. side note, how i afforded this monitor: when i bought my 480 hertz monitor there was a deal where you could get like $75 off if you used some buy now pay it later service so i did that but then paid it off basically instantly and then also it came with an rog mouse which was brand new and i didn't wireless | $159.99 modified g pro superlight mouse i've customized my g pro superlight with a hotswap pcb board, ttc 60 million gold switches, a bandaid mod for the side buttons, a weight reduction mod, and wallhack obsidian dot skates. the hotswap pcb works great and is compatible with the stock superlight scroll wheel. the scroll wheel steps feel much more distinct and less mushy compared to stock. i really enjoy the ttc gold 60m switches, they feel significantly faster than the stock ones. having a hotswap pcb is a huge plus since it lets me try different switches anytime without needing to solder. the bandaid mod involves cutting small pieces of a bandaid and placing them under the side button switches. this improves the feel, making the clicks more responsive and reducing the actuation distance. for weight reduction, i removed excess plastic using a wire cutter and a handheld rotary tool. i also took out the powerplay module and trimmed unnecessary plastic around the frame. i've used stock skates for a few years and tried tiger ice skates for a while. both performed well, but after upgrading to a glass mouse pad, i needed something more durable. the wallhack obsidian dot skates feel similar to tiger ice in terms of friction, but since they have a much smaller surface area, they glide more smoothly. the obsidian skates package includes plenty of extra skates, so i’m not too worried about wear and tear. wallhack obsidian dot skates, packaging also added a magnetic micro usb charger. this plugs into the existing port and allows the mouse to easily connect to a magnetic charger without having to manually align the original charger. this makes it extremely easy to plug in and encourages me to plug in my mouse when not using it. it does add around a gram of weight to the front of the mouse but the convenience of easily plugging in the mouse is more than worth the added weight. i'm using the stock battery. i really considered swapping out the battery for a smaller and lighter alternative but i really enjoyed only having to charge the mouse like once a week, so decided to stick with the stock battery. before mods, stock superlight mod entries.text: mouse pad, wallhack sp-004 | gear | owen miner ← gear - mouse pad: disclosure some links on this page are affiliate links. if you buy through them, owen miner may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. that support helps fund content on this website and social media. as an amazon associate i earn from qualifying purchases. wallhack sp-004 | $119.00 so far, this glass mousepad has done everything i need it to do. it might sound a little crazy, but the main reason i got this mousepad is because of how easy it is to clean. a traditional mousepad is a magnet for dust and grime, which i have found to seriously affect the consistency of my aim. a glass mousepad is extremely easy to wipe off with a microfiber cloth, and i always keep a few handy next to my desk. the base of this mousepad is great, it does not move around at all and will not damage the desk. i do think that the "performance" of a glass mousepad is overrated and that the skates on your mouse itself have a larger effect on the speed and friction while moving your mouse. one annoyance that i have heard other people talk about, and that i agree with, is how loud it is when swiping with your mouse. it may seem ridiculous to complain about the sound of a $120 mousepad, but with open-back headphones, it is loud enough to cover up some important but quiet footsteps in counter-strike. overall, i think that this mousepad was worth the high price because of its easy-to-clean surface, and it shouldn't need to be replaced as often as a traditional mousepad. wallhack glass mouse pad with g pro superlight sitting on top

entries.snippet: DeerRun under-desk walking pad: powered use retired after motor heat and belt debris; unplugged backwards walking; winter miles and belt-adjustment notes from when it still ran.
entries.text: walking pad, deerrun walking pad | gear | owen miner deerrun under-desk walking pad: powered use retired after motor heat and belt debris; unplugged backwards walking; winter miles and belt-adjustment notes from when it still ran. ← gear - walking pad: disclosure some links on this page are affiliate links. if you buy through them, owen miner may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. that support helps fund content on this website and social media. as an amazon associate i earn from qualifying purchases. deerrun walking pad | $129.99 update: powered use retired this deerrun unit is officially out of commission as a powered treadmill. the motor was running dangerously hot, there was a burning smell, and black debris was coming off the small internal drive belt. i do not plug it in anymore. i still get use out of it as a manual backwards-walking platform, the deck free-wheels when it is unplugged, so i can push the belt with my feet. that idea is in the same lane as what people cite from ben patrick (“knees over toes guy”) for low-load knee and ankle work; not medical advice, just what i am experimenting with at home. i ordered a replacement walking pad from aliexpress and will run that one powered once it arrives; this page will get a follow-up when that unit is in the rotation. when it still ran this walkpad was a huge help during cold iowa winters when i did not want to be outside. i could still get steps in without bundling up for a walk around the block. i also liked using it for short walks before or after eating. i first heard the idea on a health podcast, easy movement around meals for digestion and steadier glucose responses (not medical advice, just what i tried). i aim for something like fifteen minutes before or after a meal when i remember; honestly i have been slacking on that habit lately and want to get back to it, on whatever powered replacement i end up using day to day. i used to walk on it when doing light productivity tasks, watching youtube, or a movie. i liked the lowest setting for productive work; for movies i would put it somewhere between 1.5 and 2.2 mph, which at the higher end could work up a sweat after a mile or two. during winters while it was healthy, i would try to get five miles a day throughout the day, usually in increments of 1–2 miles. even with the motor failure, i still think the purchase paid for itself in extra activity while it was safe to run powered, and the frame is still useful unplugged until the new pad shows up. when the belt slipped, and later, the motor i did run into a maintenance headache once: the small internal drive belt wandered off center, and the walking belt got so loose it would try to stop on every step. i tore the unit apart, adjusted everything, and got it running smoothly again. eventually the motor ran hot enough to smell like fire, with black debris shedding off the internal drive belt. i opened it up multiple times trying to save it before retiring powered use entirely. photos below are from those teardown attempts. if yours acts up, there are two screws at the motor end, one pulls the motor housing tight to the frame, and the other tweaks drive-belt tension. on the opposite end, two more screws adjust left and right tension on the deck belt so you can tighten it evenly and nudge the belt back to center. screw layout after i had mine opened up, motor side vs deck belt side. deerrun walking pad underside showing screw locations for motor mount, drive belt tension, and left-right deck belt adjustment deerrun walking pad opened, motor and drive belt area deerrun treadmill internals during repair attempt deerrun drive belt wear close-up

wheels on every piece of furniture, or basically anything touching the ground in my apartment: couch, bed, tables, storage, maybe even trash cans. i want everything to be easy to move whenever i want the jattebo feet are screwed in, so it should be pretty easy to remove them and plug in threaded casters. i can use the metal connection points near the storage section to lock the pieces in place when i want a normal couch layout, or release them when i want to move things around. i can also detach the seat section from the back support and use it as a footrest. notes govee stringlight backdrop (behind grass wall) govee smart curtain lights | ~$30-60 accent lighting idea add govee stringlights behind the grass wall to create a cleaner backdrop glow and more depth. notes light switch robot switch-style robots / smart toggles | prices vary make dumb wall switches smart without rewiring add a small robot or smart actuator on top of regular rocker or toggle switches so lights can run on schedules, scenes, or voice from an app, no electrician, no replacing the whole switch plate if the wiring is fine but the switch is “dumb.” notes smart air purifiers levoit core 400s | ~$189 cleaner air around the house add smart air purifiers to improve air quality and make it easier to monitor and control from an app. the levoit core 400s has app control and a good hepa filter. notes air quality monitor airthings view plus | ~$299 track pm2.5, vocs, and co2 add an air quality monitor to track room conditions and better tune purifier speed and runtime. the airthings view plus tracks pm2.5, co2, vocs, radon, humidity, and temp all in one unit. notes full metrics stack (wearables + environment) huberman lab, michael snyder on wearables & biology | podcast “cyborg mode” without going full sci-fi i keep thinking about the huberman lab episode with dr. michael snyder where they talk about layering wearables and sensors to actually see your own baselines, the kind of setup where you’re basically wearing half a lab. i want that vibe at home: fitbit or similar for daily movement, apple watch for wrist metrics, a continuous glucose monitor when it makes sense, plus room-level air quality (see the airthings card above) so sleep, recovery, and environment aren’t all guesses. not medical advice, just the upgrade list energy of remembering that episode and wanting stronger step up in anc, comfort for long sessions, and transparency or multipoint where it actually holds up. still comparing flagships vs value tier before i lock in a model. notes automated plant care system auto watering systems | prices vary keep plants healthier with less manual work add an automated plant care system for watering schedules, moisture tracking, and healthier plant growth. tb cables | research in-wall pass-through & plate hardware | search use the pc from any room without moving it i want optical thunderbolt (or the same idea over usb-c) available at wall drops i can plug into for monitors, microphones, docks, capture, or whatever. whole-house access to one machine without lugging the pc around. notes under-monitor shelf / riser monitor risers & shelves | search usb-c hubs + sd readers | search more desk space and cleaner cable routing add an under-monitor shelf or riser so the monitor lifts up and i get usable surface back , good for stashing small gear and routing cables behind or through the shelf instead of across the whole desk. i would definitely like built-in or easy-to-mount ports: usb-c, regular usb-a, and sd card slots so card dumps and phone/laptop hookups live in one tidy front row instead of crawling behind the pc. notes wi-fi occupancy sensing router linksys aware mesh | ~$299+ get alerts if motion is detected while i am out use a wi-fi sensing router setup like a security cam alternative: if i am out running errands and person-level motion is detected in the apartment, send an alert to my phone so i can respond quickly.
